(CNN) -- At 44-years-old Abhisit Vejjajiva is Thailand's youngest prime minister in more than 60 years. But perhaps more immediately significantly, he is the country's third prime minister in four months after a period of immense upheaval in Thailand. After just two days of taking office, Thai PM Abhisit Vejjajiva talked to CNN's Dan Rivers for Talk Asia. Thailand's recent political turmoil, which included national demonstrations and the forced closures of international airports, dates back to the 2006 coup that overthrew former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, the former People's Power Party leader. In September, the Constitutional Court forced out his replacement Samak Sundaravej, finding that he had violated the constitution by appearing as a paid guest on a television cooking show. In turn he was replaced by Thaksin's brother-in-law, Somchai Wongsawat, who immediately found himself beset by opposition demonstrations that accused him of leading a proxy government for Thaksin. He too was thrown out by a Constitutional Court ruling. Abhisit was named as the new Prime Minister on December 15, and his biggest challenge will be to steady a country that until recently was known as one of the most region's most stable. A career politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle in the north east of England to wealthy Thai-Chinese parents and attended Eton, one of the UK's top private schools before studying politics, philosophy and economics at Oxford University. While highly critical of the corruption and cronyism in Thai politics, Abhisit's own route to power has not been as he may have wanted it. As leader of the Democrat Party since 2005, he failed to win either of the elections he contended. He was chosen by the Thai parliament to be Prime Minister during a special session. His selection was contingent on support of factions from the now banned PPP who changed allegiance, many of whom he had previously criticized. Abhisit now leads a coalition government with a small majority consisting of a number of parties and interests, leading political commentators to speculate about the length of his tenure in office, many suggesting more than a year in power would be a success. Countering accusations of inexperience, Abhisit can still boast 17 years of political practice, having become a parliamentarian at the age of 27. As well as being young and cosmopolitan, he has gained a reputation as being above the sleaze and corruption that has dogged many other Thai politicians, while he publicly opposed the bloodless military coup that removed Thaksin from office 2006. However critics have said that his policies are borrowed heavily from Thaksin and that his party's decision to boycott the snap election in 2006 led to the constitutional crisis and coup against Thaksin. Most of Abhisit's support comes from the educated middle classes and gaining support, or at least lessening the divisions between sections of Thai society is something he has been immediately faced with. "He needs to send a clear signal of change that he is a leader who will reach out to all," said Bunranaj Smutharak, a spokesman for Abhisit's Democrat Party. "We are confident the long turmoil over the past two years will be brought to an end by this change in government," he said. "What we set out to do is reunite the country."

In September, the Constitutional Court forced out his replacement, Samak Sundaravej, after finding that he had violated the constitution by appearing as a paid guest on a television cooking show.

Samak was, in turn, replaced by Thaksin’s brother-in-law, Somchai Wongsawat, who immediately found himself beset by opposition demonstrations accusing him of leading a proxy government for Thaksin. He, too, was removed by a Constitutional Court ruling.

A career politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle, in northeast England, to wealthy Thai-Chinese parents. He attended Eton, one of the United Kingdom’s leading private schools, before studying politics, philosophy and economics at Oxford University.

Although highly critical of corruption and cronyism in Thai politics, Abhisit’s own path to power has not unfolded as he might have wished. As leader of the Democrat Party since 2005, he failed to win either of the elections he contested.

He was chosen by the Thai Parliament to serve as prime minister during a special session. His selection depended on the support of factions from the now-banned PPP that had switched allegiances, many of which he had previously criticized.

Abhisit now leads a coalition government with a narrow majority comprising a number of parties and interests. This has prompted political commentators to speculate about the likely length of his tenure, with many suggesting that remaining in power for more than a year would constitute a success.

Countering accusations of inexperience, Abhisit can point to 17 years in politics, having become a parliamentarian at the age of 27.

In addition to being young and cosmopolitan, he has earned a reputation for remaining above the sleaze and corruption that have dogged many other Thai politicians. He also publicly opposed the bloodless military coup that removed Thaksin from office in 2006.

Critics, however, have said that his policies borrow heavily from Thaksin’s and that his party’s decision to boycott the snap election in 2006 contributed to the constitutional crisis and the coup against Thaksin.

Most of Abhisit’s support comes from the educated middle classes. Gaining broader support—or at least reducing divisions among different sections of Thai society—is therefore an immediate challenge.

“He needs to send a clear signal of change that he is a leader who will reach out to all,” said Bunranaj Smutharak, a spokesman for Abhisit’s Democrat Party.

“We are confident the long turmoil over the past two years will be brought to an end by this change in government,” he said. “What we set out to do is reunite the country.”

(CNN) — At age 44, Abhisit Vejjajiva became Thailand’s youngest prime minister in more than six decades. More immediately notable, however, was that he was the third person to hold the post in just four months, following a period of severe political instability. Two days after assuming office, Abhisit spoke with CNN’s Dan Rivers for *Talk Asia*.

Thailand’s recent crisis—which featured nationwide protests and the forced shutdown of international airports—can be traced to the 2006 military coup that removed former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who had led the People’s Power Party (PPP).

In September, the Constitutional Court dismissed Thaksin’s successor, Samak Sundaravej, after ruling that his paid appearances on a television cooking program violated the constitution. Samak was then succeeded by Thaksin’s brother-in-law, Somchai Wongsawat. Somchai immediately faced opposition protests and allegations that his administration was merely acting on Thaksin’s behalf. A Constitutional Court decision eventually removed him from office as well.

Abhisit was appointed prime minister on December 15. His primary task was to restore stability to a country that, until recently, had been regarded as one of the region’s most politically stable nations.

A lifelong politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle, in northeastern England, to affluent Thai-Chinese parents. He studied at Eton, one of Britain’s most prestigious private schools, before reading politics, philosophy and economics at Oxford University.

Although Abhisit had frequently condemned corruption and political favoritism in Thailand, his own rise to the premiership did not occur in the way he might have preferred. He had led the Democrat Party since 2005 but failed to win either of the elections in which he competed. Instead, Parliament selected him as prime minister during a special session.

His victory depended on the backing of factions from the now-outlawed PPP that switched sides, including several figures whom Abhisit had previously criticized. He consequently headed a multiparty coalition with only a narrow majority and a variety of competing interests. Political analysts therefore questioned how long his government could survive, with many suggesting that remaining in office for more than a year would itself count as an achievement.

Despite claims that he lacked experience, Abhisit had already spent 17 years in politics, having entered Parliament at 27. His youth and international background were accompanied by a reputation for remaining untouched by the scandal and corruption associated with many other Thai politicians. He had also publicly opposed the bloodless 2006 military coup that ousted Thaksin.

Critics, however, argued that many of Abhisit’s policies were heavily based on Thaksin’s. They also claimed that the Democrat Party’s boycott of the 2006 snap election helped trigger the constitutional crisis that culminated in the coup against Thaksin.

Abhisit’s strongest backing came from educated members of the middle class. One of the first challenges he faced was expanding his support—or, at minimum, reducing the deep divisions among different groups in Thai society.

“He needs to demonstrate clearly that things will change and that he intends to engage with everyone,” said Bunranaj Smutharak, a spokesperson for Abhisit’s Democrat Party.

“We believe this change of government will bring the prolonged turmoil of the past two years to a close,” he added. “Our objective is to bring the country back together.”

At 44, Abhisit Vejjajiva became Thailand’s youngest prime minister in more than six decades—and the country’s third leader in just four months. Polished, Oxford-educated and fluent in English, the Democrat Party leader presented himself as a calm, reform-minded figure capable of guiding Thailand out of one of the most turbulent periods in its recent history. Yet the complicated route that brought him to office also raised immediate questions about the strength and legitimacy of his government.

Abhisit’s rise followed years of conflict between supporters and opponents of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. Thaksin, a billionaire telecommunications entrepreneur, won broad support among rural and working-class voters through populist policies, but was accused by critics of corruption, abuse of power and weakening Thailand’s institutions. In September 2006, the military removed him in a coup while he was abroad.

The coup did not end Thaksin’s political influence. When elections were held in December 2007, the People Power Party, widely viewed as aligned with him, won the largest number of seats. Abhisit’s Democrats again fell short, reinforcing their image as a party with strong support among Bangkok’s middle class and voters in southern Thailand but limited appeal in the populous north and northeast.

The People Power Party formed a coalition government under Samak Sundaravej. His administration soon faced large demonstrations by the anti-Thaksin People’s Alliance for Democracy, whose yellow-shirted supporters occupied government facilities and demanded his removal. In September 2008, the Constitutional Court forced Samak from office after ruling that his paid appearances on a television cooking program violated conflict-of-interest rules.

Samak was replaced by Somchai Wongsawat, Thaksin’s brother-in-law, but the political crisis deepened. Anti-government protesters occupied Bangkok’s two main airports, disrupting travel, damaging tourism and attracting worldwide attention. The standoff ended only after another court decision dissolved the governing People Power Party and barred several of its leaders from politics for electoral violations. Somchai was removed from office, creating another scramble to form a government.

Abhisit finally secured the premiership in December 2008, not through a new national election but through a parliamentary vote. His Democrats assembled a majority with the help of smaller parties and defectors from the former governing coalition, including politicians who had previously supported Thaksin-aligned administrations. The shift gave Abhisit enough votes to become prime minister, but it also left him dependent on former rivals whose loyalty could not be taken for granted.

That dependence exposed the central weakness of his mandate. Although his supporters argued that his election by Parliament was fully constitutional, opponents said political pressure and behind-the-scenes maneuvering had overturned the result of the 2007 election. Thaksin’s supporters, many of whom later mobilized as the red-shirt movement, viewed Abhisit’s government as the product of court interventions, elite influence and shifting alliances rather than a direct popular choice.

Abhisit rejected the suggestion that his government lacked legitimacy. He emphasized that Thailand’s parliamentary system allowed lawmakers to choose a new prime minister when an administration collapsed and promised to govern for the entire country, including regions where the Democrats had repeatedly lost elections. He also sought to distance himself from military rule, presenting civilian government and parliamentary politics as the best way forward.

His personal history helped shape that image. Born in Britain and educated at Eton College and Oxford University, Abhisit entered Thai politics at a young age and rose steadily through the Democrat Party. Admirers saw him as intelligent, articulate and relatively untainted by corruption. Critics portrayed him as a representative of Thailand’s urban and privileged establishment, disconnected from the rural voters who had kept Thaksin-linked parties in power at the ballot box.

Once in office, Abhisit faced challenges far greater than forming a Cabinet. Thailand remained deeply divided between competing political movements, while confidence in elections, courts, the military and other national institutions had been badly damaged. The global economic downturn threatened exports and employment, and the airport seizures had dealt a serious blow to tourism. Continuing unrest in the Muslim-majority southern provinces added another long-running security problem.

Abhisit’s coalition therefore began with little room for error. He needed to keep together parties with conflicting interests, respond to voters who believed their electoral choices had been disregarded, revive the economy and prevent renewed street protests. Any defection by coalition partners—or another intervention by courts, protesters or the military—could destabilize his administration.

His ascent symbolized both the possibility of a new beginning and the unresolved nature of Thailand’s crisis. Abhisit offered youth, international experience and a promise of cleaner, more measured government. But he took power only after a coup, multiple court rulings, mass demonstrations and a dramatic rearrangement of parliamentary loyalties. Whether he could turn that fragile coalition into a stable government would depend not only on his leadership, but also on his ability to rebuild trust in a political system that many Thais believed had repeatedly failed them.

# Abhisit Vejjajiva: Oxford-educated leader takes charge of a divided Thailand

**BANGKOK, Thailand, December 2008** — Polished, soft-spoken and educated at Britain’s most prestigious schools, Abhisit Vejjajiva presents a striking contrast to the street protests, court rulings and political upheaval that propelled him into Thailand’s top job.

The 44-year-old leader of the Democrat Party was elected prime minister by parliament on December 15, ending months of uncertainty that had left Thailand with three prime ministers in as many months.

But Abhisit assumes office with his mandate already under challenge. His opponents say he reached power through political maneuvering rather than a national election, while his supporters portray him as a clean, steady figure capable of restoring confidence after a year of turmoil.

## From England to Thai politics

Abhisit was born in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, in 1964, into a prominent Thai family. He was educated at Eton College before studying philosophy, politics and economics at Oxford University. He later earned a master’s degree in economics at Oxford and taught briefly before entering Thai politics.

Fluent in English and known for his measured speaking style, Abhisit has long appealed to Bangkok’s middle class, business community and establishment voters. Critics, however, have said his privileged background leaves him disconnected from Thailand’s poorer rural majority.

He entered parliament in 1992 as one of its youngest members and served in several government posts, including as a minister attached to the prime minister’s office. In 2005, he became leader of the Democrat Party, Thailand’s oldest political party.

For years, however, the Democrats struggled to defeat parties allied with former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, the telecommunications billionaire whose populist policies built a powerful following in the north and northeast.

## A path opened by the courts

Abhisit’s route to power began with the 2006 military coup that removed Thaksin, who was later convicted of corruption and went into exile. Yet Thaksin’s allies returned to government after elections in December 2007, demonstrating the durability of his support.

The resulting administration was besieged by the anti-Thaksin People’s Alliance for Democracy, whose yellow-shirted protesters occupied government offices and, in late 2008, seized Bangkok’s two main airports. The shutdown stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers and damaged Thailand’s tourism-dependent economy.

On December 2, the Constitutional Court dissolved the ruling People Power Party and two coalition partners for electoral fraud. Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat, Thaksin’s brother-in-law, and other party executives were barred from politics.

The ruling triggered a dramatic realignment in parliament. Several former government allies and a faction of lawmakers previously aligned with Thaksin switched sides, giving Abhisit enough votes to form a coalition.

He defeated former police chief Pracha Promnok by 235 votes to 198 in the parliamentary ballot and was formally endorsed by King Bhumibol Adulyadej two days later.

Abhisit denied that the military had engineered his victory, but Thaksin’s supporters accused army leaders and establishment figures of pressuring lawmakers to join the Democrat-led coalition.

## A country split by color and class

The new prime minister inherits a nation divided between rival political movements.

The yellow-shirted PAD draws much of its support from Bangkok’s middle class, royalists and sections of the traditional elite. Its members accuse Thaksin and his allies of corruption and abuse of power.

The red-shirted United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship, meanwhile, represents many Thaksin supporters, including rural and working-class voters who say repeated court interventions and the 2006 coup have overturned their electoral choices.

For them, Abhisit’s appointment is not a return to democracy but another transfer of power arranged outside the ballot box.

Abhisit has promised national reconciliation, economic recovery and an end to political violence. He must also restore confidence after the airport occupations, address unrest in Thailand’s Muslim-majority south and shield the country from the widening global financial crisis.

His greatest challenge may be legitimacy. Abhisit brings youth, international polish and a reputation for personal integrity to the premiership. But he now has to prove that he can govern beyond the Bangkok establishment—and persuade millions of Thais who did not vote for his coalition that he is their prime minister too.

# Abhisit Vejjajiva’s Premiership Began Amid Crisis—and Was Soon Tested by Protest, Recession and Questions of Legitimacy

**BANGKOK —** Abhisit Vejjajiva, an Oxford-educated leader of Thailand’s Democrat Party, became prime minister in December 2008 promising to restore stability after years of political turmoil. Instead, his government faced a global economic downturn, an emboldened opposition movement, a divided electorate and some of the deadliest political violence in modern Thai history.

Born in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, in 1964 to Thai parents, Abhisit was educated at Eton College and the University of Oxford. He entered Thailand’s Parliament in 1992 and rose through the Democrat Party, one of the country’s oldest political organizations. He became party leader in 2005 and, at age 44, was elected prime minister by Parliament on Dec. 15, 2008, making him Thailand’s youngest head of government in more than six decades.

His polished manner, international education and reputation as a policy-oriented politician initially distinguished him from many of his rivals. But the circumstances of his ascent immediately created a problem that would follow him throughout his premiership: many Thais questioned whether his government possessed a genuine democratic mandate.

## A Contested Path to Power

Abhisit did not take office after winning a national election. His Democrat-led coalition was formed after Thailand’s Constitutional Court dissolved the governing People Power Party, which was aligned with former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra, over electoral violations.

The ruling removed Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat and barred several senior politicians from office. A group of lawmakers then switched sides, enabling Abhisit to secure a parliamentary majority.

His supporters described the transfer as constitutional and necessary after months of disruption, including anti-government “yellow shirt” protests that culminated in the occupation of Bangkok’s two main airports. His opponents, however, argued that the coalition had been assembled with help from the military and conservative establishment rather than through a fresh election.

That perception was particularly damaging in Thailand’s populous north and northeast, where parties associated with Thaksin had repeatedly won strong electoral support. Many voters there viewed Abhisit as the beneficiary of court interventions, military influence and elite resistance to the Thaksin political movement.

## The Red Shirts Take to the Streets

The most serious challenge came from the United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship, commonly known as the “red shirts.” The movement included Thaksin supporters, rural voters, pro-democracy activists and others who believed elected governments had been repeatedly undermined by military coups and judicial action.

In April 2009, red-shirt protests forced the cancellation of an Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the resort city of Pattaya after demonstrators broke into the meeting venue. The government declared a state of emergency, and troops were deployed in Bangkok to disperse protesters.

The confrontation was a warning of a much larger crisis to come.

In March 2010, tens of thousands of red-shirt demonstrators gathered in Bangkok to demand that Abhisit dissolve Parliament and call an immediate election. Protesters occupied major commercial areas in the capital, disrupting businesses and traffic for weeks.

Negotiations failed. Clashes between security forces and protesters escalated, and the government authorized military operations to clear the streets. By the time the demonstrations ended in May, roughly 90 people had been killed and about 2,000 injured. Those killed included protesters, soldiers, bystanders, rescue workers and journalists.

The bloodshed became the defining event of Abhisit’s administration.

His government said armed militants were operating among demonstrators and that security forces had to restore order. Protest leaders and human-rights groups accused the authorities of using excessive and, in some cases, lethal force. Questions about command responsibility and accountability continued long after Abhisit left office.

## An Economy Hit by Global Recession and Domestic Unrest

Abhisit also inherited an economy weakened by the 2008 global financial crisis. Thailand’s export-dependent industries were hit by falling international demand, while tourism suffered from airport closures, street protests and repeated warnings about political instability.

His government introduced stimulus programs intended to support household incomes and revive domestic spending. These included cash payments, subsidies, free public services for some lower-income residents and the “Thai Khem Khaeng,” or “Strong Thailand,” infrastructure program.

The measures helped soften the downturn, and the economy later rebounded as global conditions improved. But the government faced criticism over public spending, allegations of uneven implementation and the difficulty of delivering long-term reform while managing an unstable coalition.

Abhisit also attempted to broaden social programs, including initiatives involving education, pensions and health workers. Yet his policy agenda was repeatedly overshadowed by street conflict and disputes over the government’s legitimacy.

## A Fragile Coalition and Powerful Institutions

Maintaining control of a multiparty coalition was another persistent challenge. Abhisit depended on smaller parties and political factions whose support could not always be taken for granted. Cabinet disputes and corruption allegations complicated efforts to present the government as clean and unified.

At the same time, Thailand’s military remained an influential political actor. The army had overthrown Thaksin in a 2006 coup and played a central role in internal security during Abhisit’s term.

Although Abhisit was formally in charge of the civilian government, critics questioned how much authority he exercised over military commanders. His dependence on the armed forces during the 2010 protests reinforced claims that his administration was closely tied to the military-backed establishment.

## Southern Insurgency and Border Fighting

Beyond Bangkok’s political crisis, Abhisit’s government had to contend with a continuing separatist insurgency in Thailand’s predominantly Muslim southern provinces. Bombings, shootings and attacks on civilians, officials and security personnel continued despite efforts to adjust policy and improve administration.

The conflict, rooted in local identity, political grievances and distrust of the central government, proved resistant to a military solution. Abhisit spoke of development and greater sensitivity toward local communities, but violence persisted.

His administration also faced rising tension with neighboring Cambodia over territory near the ancient Preah Vihear temple. Thai and Cambodian troops exchanged fire in disputed border areas, causing military and civilian casualties and forcing residents to flee. The dispute fed nationalist sentiment on both sides and exposed Abhisit to pressure from hard-line groups at home.

## Defeat at the Ballot Box

Abhisit eventually dissolved Parliament and called an election for July 2011. The vote gave the public a direct opportunity to judge his government.

The Democrat Party was decisively defeated by the Pheu Thai Party, led by Yingluck Shinawatra, Thaksin’s younger sister. Pheu Thai’s victory demonstrated the continuing electoral strength of the Shinawatra-aligned movement, particularly outside Bangkok and southern Thailand.

Abhisit accepted the result and stepped down as Democrat Party leader, though he was later returned to the post. Yingluck became Thailand’s first female prime minister.

Abhisit remained active in politics for years afterward but resigned as Democrat leader again following the party’s poor showing in the 2019 general election. He has continued to be identified with the party’s more liberal and parliamentary wing, even as Thailand’s political landscape has shifted.

## A Premiership Defined by Thailand’s Divide

Abhisit’s supporters remember him as an articulate parliamentarian who took office during an extraordinarily difficult period and sought to preserve constitutional government while confronting unrest and economic danger. They point to his administration’s stimulus measures, social policies and eventual decision to hold an election.

His critics argue that his government was compromised from the beginning by the way it was formed and that its handling of the 2010 demonstrations inflicted lasting damage on its democratic credentials.

Ultimately, Abhisit’s time as prime minister reflected Thailand’s deeper political struggle: a conflict between electoral majorities and powerful unelected institutions, between Bangkok-centered elites and provincial voters, and between rival visions of how political authority should be won and exercised.

He entered office promising reconciliation. By the time he left in 2011, Thailand remained as deeply divided as ever, and the unresolved consequences of that division continued to shape the country’s politics for years.

### Background: Abhisit Vejjajiva

Abhisit Vejjajiva became Thailand’s prime minister in December 2008, taking office after more than two years of political upheaval that exposed deep divisions within the country.

The turmoil began in September 2006, when the military overthrew Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra while he was abroad. Thaksin’s allies later returned to power through elections, but their governments were short-lived. Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej was removed in September 2008 after the Constitutional Court ruled that his paid appearances on television cooking programs violated the constitution. His successor, Somchai Wongsawat, was forced from office three months later when the court dissolved the governing People Power Party over electoral fraud.

Following the ruling, defections and a realignment of parliamentary support allowed Abhisit, leader of the opposition Democrat Party, to assemble a coalition. Parliament elected him prime minister on December 15, 2008. His opponents argued that the change of government had been engineered by powerful military and establishment figures, while his supporters presented it as a constitutional transfer of power.

Born in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, in 1964, Abhisit was educated at Eton College before studying philosophy, politics and economics at the University of Oxford. He later earned a master’s degree in economics from Oxford and taught at Thailand’s Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy.

Abhisit entered parliament in 1992 as a Democrat Party member and went on to hold several government and party positions. He became leader of the Democrats in 2005, building a reputation as an articulate, internationally educated politician and a proponent of parliamentary government.

His premiership began amid continuing street protests, economic uncertainty and a bitter struggle between supporters and opponents of Thaksin. Those divisions—and questions about the durability and legitimacy of Abhisit’s coalition—formed the central challenge facing Thailand’s new leader.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how Abhisit Vejjajiva became Thailand’s third prime minister in four months and assess the strengths, controversies, and stability of his coalition government.
counterfactuals.output:
Abhisit Vejjajiva became Thailand’s third prime minister in roughly four months through a rapid sequence of judicial removals, party dissolutions, defections, and parliamentary coalition-building rather than a general election.

### How he came to power

1. **Samak Sundaravej was removed in September 2008.**  
   Samak, leader of the pro-Thaksin People Power Party (PPP), lost office when the Constitutional Court ruled that his paid appearances on television cooking programs violated rules barring ministers from outside employment.

2. **Somchai Wongsawat replaced him but lasted less than three months.**  
   Somchai—Thaksin Shinawatra’s brother-in-law—became prime minister while the anti-Thaksin People’s Alliance for Democracy (PAD) intensified its protests, eventually occupying Bangkok’s airports.

3. **The courts dissolved the governing PPP in December 2008.**  
   The Constitutional Court found the PPP and two coalition parties guilty of electoral fraud, dissolved them, and banned senior executives, including Somchai, from politics for five years. Deputy prime minister Chaovarat Charnvirakul briefly served as acting prime minister.

4. **Abhisit assembled a new parliamentary majority.**  
   The Democrat Party had not won the 2007 election, but several former government allies switched sides. Most important was the faction associated with Newin Chidchob, whose members later formed the core of the Bhumjaithai Party. Smaller parties also joined. On 15 December, the House elected Abhisit prime minister by **235 votes to 198**, and he was formally appointed two days later.

Military leaders, especially army commander Anupong Paochinda, were widely reported to have helped persuade or pressure factions to back Abhisit. Although the precise degree of military intervention remains disputed, the negotiations reinforced the perception that his government had been created by an establishment-led “backroom” realignment.

## Strengths of the coalition

- **A real parliamentary majority:** Abhisit was constitutionally elected by the House and initially commanded enough votes to govern.
- **Support from powerful institutions:** His government enjoyed comparatively favorable relations with the military, bureaucracy, palace-centered establishment, urban middle class, and much of the business community.
- **Broader regional reach:** The Democrats were strongest in Bangkok and the South, while Newin’s faction supplied MPs and local networks in the Northeast, where the Democrats were weak.
- **Experienced leadership and international credibility:** Abhisit was articulate, Western-educated, and presented himself as a moderate constitutional politician. His government also introduced stimulus and welfare measures during the global financial crisis, including cash payments, free public services, and income-support initiatives.
- **Capacity to survive parliamentary challenges:** Despite tensions, the coalition endured no-confidence votes and remained in office for more than two years.

## Controversies

- **Questionable democratic legitimacy:** The Democrats had lost the 2007 election. Critics argued that the electorate’s pro-Thaksin mandate had been reversed through court decisions, party bans, defections, and military influence rather than at the ballot box.
- **Accusations of judicial and institutional double standards:** Red-shirt supporters believed courts and other state institutions acted aggressively against pro-Thaksin parties while treating the PAD more leniently, despite its occupation of Government House and Bangkok’s airports.
- **Dependence on defectors:** The switch by Newin’s faction was seen by opponents as opportunistic and transactional. Coalition partners demanded ministries, budgets, and policy concessions in return for support.
- **Association with the PAD:** Abhisit appointed Kasit Piromya, a prominent PAD supporter, as foreign minister, deepening suspicions that the new government rewarded the movement that had helped destabilize its predecessors.
- **Repression of the Red Shirts:** Anti-government demonstrations in 2009 and especially 2010 were met with emergency rule and military force. The April–May 2010 crackdown in Bangkok left more than 90 people dead and many injured. This became the defining controversy of Abhisit’s premiership.

## How stable was it?

The coalition was **parliamentarily durable but politically fragile**.

It was stable enough to govern from December 2008 until Abhisit dissolved parliament in May 2011—far longer than either of his immediate predecessors. Support from the army and establishment, together with coalition discipline and access to state resources, helped it survive.

Yet it was never deeply secure. Its majority depended heavily on Newin-aligned MPs and smaller parties, producing continual bargaining over cabinet posts and spending. Outside parliament, the government faced severe polarization, mass Red-shirt mobilization, states of emergency, and violent confrontations. Its legitimacy remained disputed among large sections of the northern and northeastern electorate.

Thus Abhisit’s coalition achieved **institutional survival without broad political reconciliation**. Its ultimate weakness became clear in the July 2011 election, when the Democrats were decisively defeated by Yingluck Shinawatra’s Pheu Thai Party, showing that parliamentary stability had not translated into majority electoral support.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a biographical news feature about 44-year-old Abhisit Vejjajiva, emphasizing his elite British education, reputation for opposing corruption, parliamentary experience, political support base, and pledge to reunite Thailand.
counterfactuals.output:
**Oxford-educated Abhisit pledges to bridge Thailand’s political divide**

BANGKOK — At 44, Abhisit Vejjajiva embodies a polished, patrician strain of Thai politics: British-born, educated at Eton and Oxford, and known for the measured eloquence of a parliamentary debater rather than the populist theatrics of a campaign firebrand.

His rise has been built on a reputation for personal probity and opposition to corruption. Supporters present the Democrat Party leader as a clean alternative to the money politics and patronage networks that have long shaped Thai government. Critics, however, say his elite background and reliance on powerful political allies could make it difficult for him to connect with poorer rural voters.

Born in Newcastle upon Tyne to a prominent Thai family, Abhisit attended Eton College before studying philosophy, politics and economics at Oxford University. He later earned a master’s degree in economics and taught before entering public life. His fluent English, composed manner and command of policy have helped make him one of Thailand’s most internationally recognizable politicians.

Abhisit entered Parliament in 1992 and accumulated more than 16 years of legislative experience while still relatively young. He served in several parliamentary and government roles and became leader of the country’s oldest political party in 2005. From the opposition benches, he emerged as a persistent critic of former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra and of what he described as abuses of power, conflicts of interest and weakening public institutions.

His political base reflects the Democrat Party’s traditional strengths. It is strongest in Bangkok, among sections of the urban middle class, and across much of southern Thailand. Abhisit also enjoys support from business leaders, professionals and conservative voters wary of Thaksin’s influence. But the Democrats have struggled to match the electoral appeal of Thaksin-aligned parties in the populous north and northeast, where rural voters credit his governments with delivering health care, credit and other tangible benefits.

That divide is Abhisit’s central challenge. Thailand has been shaken by military intervention, court rulings, street protests and bitter competition between pro- and anti-Thaksin camps. The conflict has split regions, classes and even families, leaving many Thais doubtful that any leader can govern without deepening the confrontation.

Abhisit has pledged to change that tone. He says his mission is to restore confidence in democratic institutions, improve the economy and reunite a country exhausted by years of political turmoil.

“I want to be a prime minister for all Thai people,” he has said in outlining his approach, promising reconciliation rather than retaliation.

Whether he can deliver will depend on more than his clean image and parliamentary skill. He must persuade rural voters that he understands their economic anxieties, reassure opponents that he is not merely the acceptable face of Thailand’s traditional establishment, and hold together a potentially fragile coalition of supporters.

For Abhisit, the attributes that propelled him upward — elite schooling, intellectual polish and establishment confidence — may also be his greatest liabilities. His task is to turn the manners of an Oxford common room into a language that resonates in Thailand’s villages, markets and divided streets.
